title: ‘Sons of Anarchy’ Cast Reunites for FX Limited Series ‘Legends’
description:
The “Sons of Anarchy” are riding again! Kind of…

	FX has ordered the limited series “Legends,” which will bring much of the hit outlaw biker drama’
body:
The “Sons of Anarchy” are riding again! Kind of…

	FX has ordered the limited series “Legends,” which will bring much of the hit outlaw biker drama’s main cast back together. The series will star Charlie Hunnam (Jax), Ron Perlman (Clay), Katey Sagal (Gemma), Maggie Siff (Tara), Mark Boone Junior (Bobby), Tommy Flanagan (Chibs), Kim Coates (Tig), and Theo Rossi (Juice). 

	The logline for the show states, “When the cast of “Sons of Anarchy” reunites at a fan convention after more than a decade, the line between life and art blurs as the fractured brotherhood finds itself up against a real-world threat more dangerous than anything they ever faced in their show.” 
	

	Hunnam developed the show with Jonathan Groff (“black-ish,” “How I Met Your Mother”). Both serve as executive producers along with Rob Mac, Nicholas Frenkel, and Jackie Cohn. The series will be produced by FX Productions and 20th Television.


	“When Charlie brought us this inspired idea, we instantly sparked to his bold and entertaining vision,” said Nick Grad, FX Entertainment president. “Charlie’s talents are on full display as a writer, performer and executive producer, leading the real-life brotherhood on an adventure that is both a love letter to the series and a fun meta twist on what fans think they know.”

	“Sons of Anarchy,” which was created by Kurt Sutter, proved to be a major early hit for FX as the network was making its push into original scripted dramas nearly 20 years ago. Originally premiering in 2008, the show ran for seven seasons and nearly 100 episodes.

	Hunnam recently received the first Emmy nomination of his career for his starring role in the Netflix anthology series “Monster: The Ed Gein Story.” Aside from “Sons of Anarchy,” he also previously starred in the Apple series adaptation of the book “Shantaram” as well as shows like “Queer as Folk” and “Undeclared.” In film, he is known for roles in features including “The Gentlemen,” “Pacific Rim,” “True History of the Kelly Gang,” “Rebel Moon – Part One: A Child of Fire,” and “The Lost City of Z.”

title: Shirley MacLaine Makes Rare Video Appearance at 92 Years Old and Quips About ‘Sweet Charity’: ‘It Didn’t Do Very Well’
description:
Shirley MacLaine has made a rare video appearance at the age of 92, and she’s not shy to throw some quips at “Sweet Charity‘s” expense.

	“I would l
body:
Shirley MacLaine has made a rare video appearance at the age of 92, and she’s not shy to throw some quips at “Sweet Charity‘s” expense.

	“I would like to see ‘Sweet Charity’ again. Now, while you’re watching it, remember how hard we worked,” MacLaine said in a video posted by the Southampton Playhouse ahead of the theater’s upcoming screening of Bob Fosse’s musical film. “And between you and me, it didn’t do very well.”


	MacLaine starred in Bob Fosse’s “Sweet Charity,” which released in 1969 and was a box office flop; nevertheless, Fosse found commercial success later in his career with “Cabaret” and “All That Jazz.” In Fosse’s directorial debut, MacLaine was joined in the cast by Sammy Davis Jr., Chita Rivera, John McMartin, Paula Kelly and Ricardo Montalban.
	

	In December 2025, MacLaine received a lifetime achievement award at the first-ever Dance Hall of Fame induction ceremony. The award was also named in MacLaine’s honor.

	“Getting an award for dancing is the most important acknowledgment I could have,” she said while accepting her award. “My mother took me to dancing class when I was three because I had weak ankles and I fell in love with it.”

	MacLaine won the best actress Oscar in 1984 for her work in “Terms of Endearment.” Her previous Oscar nominations were for “The Turning Point,” “The Other Half of the Sky: A China Memoir,” “Irma la Douce,” “The Apartment” and “Some Came Running.” Her last on-screen appearance was in the 2022 film “American Dreamer” and two episodes of “Only Murders in the Building.” In November 2025, Variety exclusively announced that MacLaine and Ansel Elgort would be starring in a road trip comedy titled “Lucy Boomer.”

schema.headline: Shirley MacLaine Makes Rare Video Appearance at 92 Years Old and Quips About ‘Sweet Charity’: ‘It Didn’t Do Very Well’

title: Anne Hathaway Pushed ‘Really Hard’ to Bring Julie Andrews Back for ‘Princess Diaries 3’ but the Icon Passed: ‘Whatever She Wants, We Completely Understand’
description:
Aug 19, 2026 12:07pm PT	
	

	
		Anne Hathaway Pushed ‘Really Hard’ to Bring Julie Andrews Back for ‘Princess Diaries 3’ but the Icon P
body:
Aug 19, 2026 12:07pm PT	
	

	
		Anne Hathaway Pushed ‘Really Hard’ to Bring Julie Andrews Back for ‘Princess Diaries 3’ but the Icon Passed: ‘Whatever She Wants, We Completely Understand’
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Getty Images
	

		
	
				
	Disney may not be bringing Julie Andrews back for “Princess Diaries 3,” but it’s not for lack of trying. The offer is still on the table if Andrews ever changes her mind, according to franchise star Anne Hathaway, who will reprise the role of Mia Thermopolis in the film. 

	“First of all, I just want to say if she has a change of heart, we’re down,” Hathaway told Entertainment Tonight at D23. “But we also want to be respectful. For goodness sakes, if anybody has contributed to the world of entertainment and to our collective joy, it’s her. Whatever she wants, we completely understand. We did push really hard to see if she would want to do it.”
	

	“I just want it to be fun. The women who were six when the first one came out — a lot of whom are now mothers themselves, maybe even with six-year-olds — I want them to feel like they’re bringing their children to something that mattered to them,” Hathaway continued. 


	Andrews recently confirmed in an interview with Today that she would not be playing Queen Clarisse again. “I think I probably passed… I think I’m retired, really, would be about the best description for that,” she said. “They asked me all last year if I would be keen to do it. It was very very hard to say ‘no,’ but I did because I thought I had a wonderful ride, and this one I felt would flourish very well and wouldn’t need Granny going in there at my age.”


	
		More from Variety

schema.headline: Anne Hathaway Pushed ‘Really Hard’ to Bring Julie Andrews Back for ‘Princess Diaries 3’ but the Icon Passed: ‘Whatever She Wants, We Completely Understand’

title: Ji.hlava’s Emerging Producers 2026 Reveal Pitches for Upcoming Projects (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival has revealed to Variety the projects that the participants of its 2026 Emerging Producers program are working on.
body:
Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival has revealed to Variety the projects that the participants of its 2026 Emerging Producers program are working on. The producers were asked to deliver an elevator pitch for their projects.

	Since 2010, the festival has selected 18 up-and-coming documentary producers — 17 from Europe and one from outside the continent (Japan is the 2026 guest country) — offering them educational, networking and promotional opportunities.
	

	The Emerging Producers portal has become a valuable resource for documentary filmmakers seeking co-producers, featuring over 250 profiles of alumni from the program.


	Here are the pitches from the 2026 lineup:

	Title: Glorious UtopiaProducers: Tomáš Gič, Katarína Krnáčová/Silverart (Slovakia)Director: Marek MoučkaGenre: DocumentarySynopsis: “Glorious Utopia” observes the citizens and kings of the unofficial microstate Elgeland-Vargaland. Through the story of two aging kings and their encounters with real social events, the film explores topics of identity, power, and the meaning of borders in current world.Pitch: Every utopia eventually meets reality. The fictional microstate Elgaland-Vargaland begins as an artistic game but evolves into a powerful lens on borders and identity. As global tensions continue to reshape our world, the story became strikingly timely, with the potential to resonate at international festivals as well as wider audiences.

	Title: MadamProducers: Pavla Klimešová & Eva Rejč/Helium Film (Czech Republic)Director: Barbora ChalupováGenre: Intimate dramaSynopsis: As dominatrix Madam Chimera, Nela is untouchable; off duty she’s a regular single 35 year old longing for love and acceptance. When two men – a potential partner and a manipulative client – enter her life, Nela has to confront her family history all while trying to decide whether to freeze her eggs.Pitch: Inspired by true events, Madam blends dark humor with emotional realism to tell a deeply human story set in the rarely explored world of professional domination. Offering a fresh female perspective on sex work, it explores love, autonomy, fertility, belonging and the search for genuine human connection.
	

	Title: Story of the Painter Who Created a PhotographerProducers: Julie Meigniez, Vincent Gazaigne/Talweg (France); Michaela Jeleneková/Arytmia (Slovakia)Director: Christian PaigneauGenre: DocumentarySynopsis: Amid the turmoil of World War II, painter Ester Šimerová and lawyer Martin Martinček endured profound personal loss. After the war, Martinček became a photographer under Šimerová’s influence. The film explores artistic inspiration, the bond between two creators, and whether art can help heal the wounds of grief.Pitch: Built from personal correspondence, archival footage, and careful fictionalization, the film brings two lesser-known artists to international audiences. Their rare artistic bond offers an intimate perspective on defining events of 20th-century Europe and Czechoslovakia, creating a hybrid documentary with broad cultural, historical and emotional appeal.

	Title: See What I Say!Producer: Ringailė Leščinskienė/Zero Copy Reel (Lithuania)Director: Artūras JevdokimovasGenre: Creative observational documentarySynopsis: What if connection began where words failed? In Bologna, Vilnius and Kyiv, deaf bartenders run the bar, and hearing visitors must adapt to order, connect and be understood. Misunderstandings, laughter and moments of fragile intimacy create a cinematic exploration of communication beyond words.Pitch: “See What I Say!” is co-authored by deaf collaborators who shape its frame, sound and rhythm — not merely consulted, but creating. Sign language becomes cinematic grammar rather than subject matter. Backed by an experienced international team and three co-producing countries, the film arrives at a moment when deaf rights have reached a global tipping point.

	Title: Argentina-Sweden-Kurdistan (working title)Producer: Caroline Drab/BCD Film (Sweden) in coproduction with Film I Väst (Sweden)Director: Viana Barzan MikkelsenGenre: Feature documentarySynopsis: Filmmaker Viana embarks on a journey across three continents with a mission to introduce her Kurdish grandmother to her Argentinian grandmother for the first time. Viana sets to understand migration and exploring the complex tapestry of her own heritage – and shortly discovers she is about to become a mother herself.Pitch: “Argentina-Sweden-Kurdistan” (working title) is an intimate documentary about understanding heritage and identity, and a relevant story for today’s increasingly globalized generation. Settling that borders and distance cannot fail to erase the affinity and care that can arise in a mere meeting.
	

	Title: CosMOSProducers: Evi Stamou/Maketa Media (Greece)Director: Yannis BererisGenre: DocumentarySynopsis: Yannis, a 25-year-old film student, documents a turbulent decade in Athens from 2010 to 2020 using one of the first affordable DSLR cameras capable of shooting video. As Greece faces the harsh realities of the financial crisis, he captures both public unrest and intimate personal moments within his circle of friends.Pitch: CosMOS is a hybrid documentary exploring the millennial generation through Greece’s financial crisis, revealing how personal memories reflect shared European experiences of precarity. The film has strong festival and theatrical potential, resonating with audiences through its themes of disillusionment, resilience and collective memory.

	Title: IntermissionProducers: Azra Djurdjevic, Michael Graf/Cloud Fog Haze Pictures (Switzerland)Director: Noëmi Steffen, Yannick MosimannGenre: Hybrid fiction featureSynopsis: After a painful breakup, a young playwright accepts a job as assistant director for a theater company in a foreign city. Seduced by artistic freedom and the promise of belonging, she gradually loses herself in a male-dominated world shaped by charisma, dependence and manipulation.Pitch: “Intermission” blends autobiography and fiction to explore belonging, power dynamics and the things we perceive long before we understand them. Shot on 16mm inside a theater, with every sound recreated in post-production, it creates a film language at the intersection of cinema and theater.

	Title: The Silence of OromayProducer: Nahusenay Dereje Ayalew/1960 Films (Ethiopia)Director: Habtamu GebrehiwotGenre: DocumentarySynopsis: In 1984, during Ethiopia’s communist Derg regime (1974–1991), celebrated novelist Bealu Girma disappeared after publishing “Oromay,” exposing the regime’s disastrous war in Eritrea. Four decades later, the investigation follows witnesses, archives, and competing narratives to uncover the truth behind his disappearance and enduring legacy.Pitch: More than a mystery, this is a gripping political thriller about censorship, war and the price of truth. Set against a conflict that transformed the Horn of Africa, the film uncovers a story with universal relevance—where literature became a battlefield and a writer paid the ultimate price.
	

	Title: Home Is a DollhouseProducer: Anna Tóth/ULab (Hungary)Director: Dorottya MártonGenre: Hybrid documentary featureSynopsis: A filmmaker turns the camera on herself and her estranged mother to explore the lingering wounds of abandonment and intergenerational silence. Weaving together personal archives, fictional reconstructions and intimate encounters, the film becomes a poetic search for understanding and asks what we inherit beyond blood.Pitch: Blending documentary, fiction and personal archives, “Home Is a Dollhouse” transforms an intimate mother-daughter story into a visually distinctive exploration of memory, migration and inherited trauma.

	Title: Listening to the WorldProducers: Eugene Rachkovsky & Olha Bregman/TABOR (Ukraine), Antonia Kilian/Pink Shadow Films (Germany), Mario Adamson & Ashley J. Smith/Sisyfos Film (Sweden)Director: Yelizaveta SmithGenre: DocumentarySynopsis: Iva can’t hear the world because of her disability. She and her son Mykyta face the war in Ukraine and are forced to flee to Germany as refugees. In Berlin, Iva gets a cochlear implant and the chance to hear again. In a world full of noises, challenges and war, Iva seeks for the way to hear and to be heard.Pitch: In a world of noise and war, Iva fights to hear and be heard. Directed by Yelizaveta Smith, an established Ukrainian voice previously selected at Berlinale and Cannes, this visually striking documentary is backed by Sundance and Eurimages, with strong partners. Now seeking a sales agent and impact partners.

	Title: 35 LettersProducer: Maria Krauss/Plesnar & Krauss Films (Germany)Director: Zuzanna SolakiewiczGenre: DocumentarySynopsis: Thirty-five unanswered letters sent by teenage girls to modelling agencies in 1990s Poland resurface decades later. Three of those girls, now mothers of adolescent daughters, rediscover their younger selves as they confront their children’s pragmatic choices. Today, as their daughters reach the same age, the film becomes their reply.Pitch: “35 Letters” turns a found archive into a cinematic dialogue across generations, showing how capitalism reshaped women’s desires, bodies and ambitions in post-socialist Poland via intimate mother-daughter stories. The film speaks of being seen, inherited dreams and the courage to find one’s own voice. Award-winning creators of “The Guest” seek an international co-producer.
	

	Title: The Pot, the Lid and the NurseProducer: Ivana Shekutkoska/Minimal Collective (North Macedonia)Co-producer: Zornitsa Sophia/MQ Pictures (Bulgaria)Director: Vardan TozijaGenre: Feature filmSynopsis: After a spectacular breakdown, a burned-out nurse takes a job caring for a warring elderly couple in a remote mountain town, only to find herself entangled in their long-buried secrets, dormant household war, and the unexpected tenderness of people at the end of their lives.Pitch: A dark comedy that turns grief into laughter and conflict into compassion. Inspired by true experiences, the film combines emotional authenticity, memorable characters and a deeply human story, offering strong international audience appeal and co-production potential.

	Title: La Gruta del VientoProducers: Angelo Rocco Troiano/Mediterraneo Cinematografica (Italy), Francisco Marquez & Andrea Testa/Pensar con Las Manos (Argentina), Ana Luz Buchi & Daniel Pech/Terciera Margem (Brazil)Director: Eduardo CrespoGenre: Immigration drama with documentary approachSynopsis: Mara returns to her father’s house in a small mountain village in Italy. Both are Argentines. Her father works as a rural veterinarian despite his poor health and while Mara accompanies him on his last work trips, she will discover about her identity thanks to a young speleologist and an immigrant guy whom they will all have to protect.Pitch: “La Gruta del Viento” is an intimate story of a father and daughter navigating their roots in the Tuscan mountains. Through grief, migration and unexpected encounters, the film explores identity, belonging and the healing power of nature. Directed with sensitivity by Eduardo Crespo, previously an IDFA and IKUSMIRA Berriak awards winner.

	Title: Tree Killers (Die Baummörder)Producer: Dominic Spitaler/Kacerovsky, AustriaDirector: Rosa FriedrichGenre: DocumentarySynopsis: If a tree is murdered and no one’s there to hear it, does it make a sound? More and more people are secretly injecting glyphosate into tree trunks to kill them. Who does this? And why? A conversational, humorous investigative documentary probes the motivation behind the hatred of innocent trees.Pitch: Director Rosa Friedrich, fresh off her premiere in Karlovy Vary, teams up with Vienna Shorts award-winner Simon Nagy to investigate. The hunt for tree killers leads the pair to ever bigger questions: Where does this hatred of nature come from? Are all tree killers fascists? And how long do trees stay stoic before they strike back? An ecological whodunit with an oddly perfect pair of detectives.
	

	Title: Let the Sea Take Away All EvilProducer: Maarten D’Hollander/Krater Films (Belgium)Co-producers: Family Affair Films (Netherlands), Naoko Films (Belgium/France), Omaja Films (Portugal), in association with Tardo Films (Brazil)Director: Laura VandewynckelGenre: Hybrid documentarySynopsis: On Itaparica island, Bahia, a planned mega-bridge threatens to swallow a community. Local artists and activists form a satirical “Creative Cabinet of Change,” deploying an animatronic horse, a speaker-puppet and the island’s condemned ferry to expose the scapegoating mechanisms that sell progress to the very people it will displace.Pitch: A playful, politically sharp hybrid documentary. Satire as resistance, performed by the people living it: real islanders stage an absurdist counter-campaign against a mega-bridge, with animatronic figures as their spokesmen. Humor makes the politics travel, a rare Brazilian story that’s joyful rather than grim, visually striking, and built for audiences activist documentaries usually can’t reach.

	Title: Shadows of SovereigntyProducer: Yann Tonnar/Manufactura Pictures (Luxembourg)Director: Yann TonnarGenre: Hybrid documentarySynopsis: As World War I devastates Europe, Luxembourg’s young Grand Duchess Marie Adelheid battles parliament, press and public opinion for power. Accused of German sympathies, she abdicates in 1919. Exiled from Bavaria to Lake Geneva to Rome, she seeks refuge in convents that reject her — dying misunderstood, at 29, in 1924.Pitch: Filmed across Bavaria, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Italy, this rarely told side of World War I follows a sheltered young monarch, barely out of childhood, thrust onto the throne and into Kaiser Wilhelm II’s shadow. A story of youth, faith, war and the fragility of power – haunting and pan-European in scope.

	Title: Dhākira: Through Qassem’s EyesProducer: Bernardo Lopes/Omaja (Portugal)Director: Balolas CarvalhoGenre: Documentary featureSynopsis: Qassem founded Ramattan, Palestine’s first independent TV news agency, and appeared on TIME’s cover during the First Intifada. Decades later, exiled in Egypt and tending a farm he planted by hand, he waits to return to Gaza and rebuild, for the fifth time, everything he has lost.Pitch: Qassem holds the last surviving audiovisual archive of Gaza before its devastation. This film weaves that footage with new images of his exile, a poetic documentary essay that refuses the urgency of breaking news. A story about what it means to keep planting when everything around you has been destroyed.
	

	Title: Grete and the Cuban PianistProducers: Anita Vedå/Smau Media & Geir Netland/Harding Film (Norway)Director: Vigdis NielsenGenre: Feature documentarySynopsis: When a chance encounter sparks an unexpected musical journey, ordinary Grete risks everything to record in New York and perform in Cuba. But as her lifelong dream finally becomes reality, an unforeseen challenge changes everything. This deeply moving film is a powerful testament to art, connection, and the human spirit.Pitch: A film for everyone who postponed a dream. Through Grete’s journey, we ask: Is it ever too late to begin? Do we only understand the value of life when faced with losing it? What happens if we never dare to try? A deeply human exploration of timing, risk and self-recognition.

title: Peacock Just Raised Its Prices — Here’s How to Get It Free With Walmart+
description:
Peacock just got more expensive, but Walmart+ members have a way around the latest price hike.

	The NBC streamer raised prices across all three of
body:
Peacock just got more expensive, but Walmart+ members have a way around the latest price hike.

	The NBC streamer raised prices across all three of its plans on Aug. 18, with its ad-supported Peacock Premium tier jumping from $10.99 to $12.99 per month, or from $109.99 to $129.99 annually. Premium Plus, which removes most ads and adds downloads, is now $19.99 per month or $199.99 per year.


	Enter Walmart+, the retailer’s $98-a-year membership program, which offers free subscriptions to Peacock and Paramount+ as one of its many perks. A Walmart+ membership costs $12.95/month, meaning an annual membership actually $31.99 cheaper than paying for a year of Peacock Premium on its own.


	Although members are only allowed to take advantage of one of the two streaming offers, savvy users online have revealed a workaround. Walmart says members are allowed to switch their included streaming provider once every 90 days. So, for example, you could choose Peacock Premium, watch it for 90 days, switch to Paramount+ Essential for the next 90 days and then switch back to Peacock once another 90-day period has elapsed. You don’t have to switch when the window opens; if you do nothing, your current service remains active.

	That makes Walmart+ particularly useful for viewers willing to plan their subscriptions around specific releases. Peacock includes next-day NBC and Bravo programming, Peacock originals, movies and a growing slate of live sports, while Paramount+ Essential ($8.99/month on its own) offers programming from CBS, Nickelodeon, MTV, Comedy Central and more, alongside Paramount films, originals and select live sports.


	To take advantage of their streaming offers, sign up for Walmart+ here.

title: How ‘The Pitt,’ ‘Widow’s Bay’ and ‘Pluribus’ Casting Directors Found Their Emmy-Worthy Town Locals, Hospital Patients and Hive Mind Members
description:
For casting directors, there is no such thing as a small part.

	Shows like “Widow’s Bay,” “Hacks,” “Pluribus” and “The Pitt” not only made an impre
body:
For casting directors, there is no such thing as a small part.

	Shows like “Widow’s Bay,” “Hacks,” “Pluribus” and “The Pitt” not only made an impression with the Television Academy across the board, but saw many of their supporting actors and guest stars land nominations. Working character actors like Kate O’Flynn, Carlos Manuel Vesga, Lauren Weedman and Patrick Ball all landed their first Emmy nominations for brief but meaty parts.
	

	So how did these Emmy-nominated shows go about finding their hospital patients, hive mind members and quirky assistants?


	With its rotating roster of hospital patients and doctors, Season 2 of “The Pitt” saw 13 of its performers get recognized — up 10 from last season. Landing a background spot on the show can provide L.A. locals consistent work for up to six months due to the show’s unique filming style.

	Casting directors Cathy Gelfond and Erica Berger, who have been working together since 2017 and won an Emmy for their work on Season 1, are responsible for casting anyone with at least one line, which totaled 250 performers this past season.

	“In my 30-plus years, I think I had done two movies and had never done a television show [in Los Angeles]. So, it’s been quite fascinating to see the depth of talent in day players,” Gelfond says. Berger adds, “We get to do every single part here, from top to bottom, so we have more opportunities to give people their first chance.”

	Many of this season’s new discoveries, including guest stars Brittany Allen and Jeff Kober, made a strong impression as hospital patients.
	



	

									Warrick Page/HBO Max
	



	“I think it’s just if we feel moved,” Berger says about what draws her to specific actors. “Because we’re watching so many of the same scenes again and again, if I’m crying after I’ve seen 40 takes of the same one, I know it’s going to move other people too.”

	When building out the quirky world of Katie Dippold’s horror comedy set on a tiny New England island, “Widow’s Bay” casting directors Allison Jones and Emily Buntyn relished the fact that nobody wanted a recognizable face. “I’m from that part of the world, you’re not going to cast glam-looking people who come from there,” Jones says.

	Jones and Buntyn, who have worked together for over a decade, were initially brought on to consult on the casting of Tom Loftus, the horror-skeptic mayor who wound up being played by Matthew Rhys (double Emmy-nominated thanks to his turn in “The Beast in Me.”).

	What struck Jones when reading Dippold’s scripts, long before anyone knew the sensation “Widow’s Bay” would become, was how she wrote the older locals in town.

	“I couldn’t wait to grab these women and men who were kind of crusty and old,” Jones says with a wide grin on her face.

	Dale Dickey, who plays the town gossip, was a no-brainer addition. Her audition was unorthodox: “The scene was her just having a coughing fit. We needed an actual smoker,” Jones says.



	

									Apple TV
	



	As a casting agent who has worked on everything from “Barbie” to “Freaks and Geeks,” Jones’ connections run deep in the industry. She happened to know O’Flynn’s manager, who had just signed her from London.

	“She physicalized it all within herself; she was extremely quiet. She did a very good American accent, but what she imparted to that character was not on the page,” Jones says of O’Flynn’s audition.

	“We had wonderful actresses read for that, many of whom could have done the part. Kate, though, was the personification of when you make a funny noise and a dog goes, ‘Huh?’”

	At the core of “Hacks” is a story about a veteran (Jean Smart) and up-and-coming comedian (Hannah Einbinder) coming together to change each other’s lives. So naturally, the fifth and final season had to go full out with a diverse, multigenerational cast to celebrate everything the show has come to represent, which included bringing back vets like Laurie Metcalf and Weedman, while introducing Cherry Jones and Leslie Bibb into the mix.
	

	“If you don’t get it right with those smaller roles in comedy, you’re dead in the water,” casting director Linda Lowy says.

	Lowy and fellow casting director Morgan Smith, who work together under their Backyard Casting banner, were excited to cast more L.A.-based talent this time around. There were also financial reasons attached to that: “We needed to find locals, and I think that’s across the board with every show now. There’s no extra money anymore,” Lowy says.

	The journey to casting Jones, who guest stars in the memorable “Montecito” episode alongside Bibb, was a difficult, touch-and-go process because of conflicts in the Emmy-winning actor’s schedule. “It just shows that if you keep going at it in the most gentle, creative, nice way, you might get what you want,” Lowy says.



	

									HBO Max
	



	The show has also been celebrated for its queer representation, with openly queer performers like Einbinder bringing their own lived experience to the characters. “Anytime that they intentionally write a queer character, we always try to prioritize those castings for authenticity,” Smith says. “We literally put it in the breakdown.”

	“Pluribus,” which was specifically written by “Breaking Bad” creator Vince Gilligan as a vehicle for Rhea Seehorn, had to find the right performers to round out the collective hive mind.

	Karolina Wydra and Vesga were two of the breakout finds for casting directors Sharon Bialy, Sherry Thomas and Russell Scott, who all worked with Gilligan on both “Breaking Bad” and “Better Call Saul.”

	“We had gotten to the point where we had seen everyone that we had thought of and had been submitted from all over the world. We finally had to go back to our old handwritten books, just looking through them,” Scott recalls. 

	That was when Wydra, who didn’t have an agent or manager at the time, popped up from an audition years ago.



	

									Apple TV
	



	Vesga’s casting came from an hour-long conversation Bialy and Scott had with him at Gelson’s after being impressed by his tape. Bialy recognized “the kind of actor” Gilligan would be drawn to for the part of Manousos.

	“He’s a really smart guy and we have found that if you cast really smart actors, you tend to get a lot more than you were even hoping for in future episodes,” Bialy says of the theater-trained performer.
	

	“One thing that’s different with the casting for Vince and these roles is you’re casting a lot of people who’ve never done it before. They might be theater actors, but they’ve never been on camera. We’re spending a long time talking to them, explaining that it’s just about listening.”

	As these casting directors reflect on their Emmy-nominated work — and their work on follow-up seasons — the search for the next breakout performer is always on.

	“It just never stops once you are submerged into this career path,” Thomas says. “If I’m watching the new ‘Descendants’ movie with my kids on the weekend, I am going, ‘Oh, my God, that’s a discovery! Wow, they’re really good.’ And I’m looking them up in the middle of having this moment with my family because my brain just won’t turn off.”

schema.headline: How ‘The Pitt,’ ‘Widow’s Bay’ and ‘Pluribus’ Casting Directors Found Their Emmy-Worthy Town Locals, Hospital Patients and Hive Mind Members

title: David Krumholtz Clarifies He’s Putting Acting Career on Hold but Not ‘Retiring or Quitting’: Disappointments ‘Are Starting to Sting More’
description: “Supergirl” and “Oppenheimer” actor David Krumholtz is clarifying his remarks from earlier this week about whether he’s retiring from acting. Krumho
body:
“Supergirl” and “Oppenheimer” actor David Krumholtz is clarifying his remarks from earlier this week about whether he’s retiring from acting. Krumholtz posted on Instagram Wednesday to explain that he never used the word “retiring” or “quitting” but that “I decided to put my career on hold” and that he feels a “burning desire” to find a way to give more of himself to others in need.

	“Firstly, I am very well. And I feel very loved,” he wrote. “I don’t expect anyone to understand, but the outpouring of support for my decision has been deeply heartwarming. I am wildly grateful, as more than one of my biggest dreams have come true as a result of being an actor. Grateful to all who support and believe in me.
	

	“However, a time has come where the weight of those dreams and ambitions has become surprisingly oppressive,” he continued. “That’s a me problem, not a Hollywood as a whole problem. There are no rules that guarantee success, but I know this: an amazing career in this business consists of a small handful of triumphs, but not without a mountain of disappointments. I love my mountain of disappointments, I do, but I’m human and my mountain is starting to sting more than it used to. Need time to figure that out, let it heal. My mental health is vital to my family. My career has run the gamut. I’m in disbelief. 


	“But I find myself at a crossroads between the inherent self involvement being a professional actor requires, and a burning desire to give more of myself to others in need, in whatever way I can. And so, for the time being, I’m pursuing that goal. There’s still more work to come. Stuff to be seen. And as always, I really hope you enjoy what I’ve put out there. Just,… gimme a sec,” he concluded.
	

	Krumholtz posted a statement on Threads on Monday, and later deleted it, saying, “I kinda sorta put my acting career on hold the other day. It’s been something I’ve been petrified to do for years. Specifically, the fear was that I’d go broke and not be able to handle being out of the game.”

	“It became clear to me this year, that if I were to continue fighting for parts (what I used to call ‘auditioning’), I’d be doing so for roles that exploit my talent and reputation for a drastically diminishing return. Exploitative art isn’t art. And artists deserve a fair pay percentage for work that assists their employers in making profits,” he wrote in the now-deleted post.

	The actor, who has also appeared on “The Studio” and “Pokerface,” has long been ambivalent about continuing his career, once telling his friend Seth Rogen he had applied to work at a car dealership.

schema.headline: David Krumholtz Clarifies He’s Putting Acting Career on Hold but Not ‘Retiring or Quitting’: Disappointments ‘Are Starting to Sting More’

title: ‘Widow’s Bay’ and Other Contenders Continue to Complicate Emmy’s Comedy Conundrum
description: You’re probably as tired of the “what’s a comedy?” debate as I am, particularly when it comes to awards shows like the Emmys. FX’s “The Bear” reigni
body:
You’re probably as tired of the “what’s a comedy?” debate as I am, particularly when it comes to awards shows like the Emmys. FX’s “The Bear” reignited that conversation a few years ago, even though it’s hardly the only show to be nominated or even win an Emmy despite it often feeling more like a drama.

	This year, the attention turned to Apple TV’s “Widow’s Bay,” one of the hottest new shows of the season. The acclaim for “Widow’s Bay” seems nearly universal, and the show’s 19 Emmy nominations prove that the buzz surrounding the show wasn’t a fluke. But again, we have to ask: Is it a comedy?
	

	“Widow’s Bay” comes from a comedy writer, “Parks and Recreation” alum Katie Dippold. And it absolutely sprinkles laugh into the horror format, particularly through the town’s quirky characters. As the misfits who make up Widow’s Bay react matter-of-factly to some of the creepy and strange goings-on around them, at the center of it all is Matthew Rhys as Mayor Tom Loftis. He bumbles his way through a secret that threatens the well-being of his small, New England-set island community.

	There’s creepy clowns, scary apparitions, undead serial killers, a wild sea hag and a terrible curse that haunts the show’s characters throughout the season — and while the laughs cut the tension, you’re still on the edge of your seat for all 10 episodes. And by the way, on its own service, Apple TV classifies “Widow’s Bay” a “mystery,” while “Ted Lasso” and “Shrinking” are labeled “comedy.”



	

	



	But in fairness to “Widow’s Bay,” are any of this year’s comedy nominees actually comedies? Most of this year’s contenders (which also include “Abbott Elementary,” “The Bear,” “Hacks,” “Margo’s Got Money Troubles,” “Nobody Wants This,” “Only Murders in the Building” and “Shrinking”) feature some heart-tugging moments that have made me tear up. I’ve said it before — the best dramas on TV are our Emmy-nominated comedies.
	

	When did comedy get so dramatic? You’ll have to go back to 1988, the year that Emmy voters nominated two single-camera shows in the outstanding comedy series category for the first time: “The Wonder Years” and “Frank’s Place.” The fact that both shows came out at the same time represented a bit of a “dramedy” revolution in primetime; previously, the genre was pretty much only devoted to multi-camera shows filmed in front of a live studio audience, like the other nominees that year: “Cheers,” “The Golden Girls” and “Night Court.”

	But “The Wonder Years” was still a half-hour show, and contained enough humorous beats that no one seriously challenged its comedy bona fides. The bigger change came in 1999, when the hourlong Fox legal dramedy “Ally McBeal” won the comedy Emmy. Sure, it had quirky moments with that dancing baby, but it could have just as easily been put in the drama bucket. (“Ally” creator David E. Kelley has the same thing this year with the quite dramatic comedy nominee “Margo’s Got Money Troubles.”) 

	When “Desperate Housewives” was nominated as a comedy in 2005, it also raised eyebrows: Did a show that opened with a death, adultery and focused so much on a dark mystery belong in the comedy path?

	Around the 2010s, the dramedy lines had blurred enough that we started to see shows hop Emmy categories: Netflix’s “Orange Is the New Black” started in comedy, then moved to drama. Showtime’s “Shameless” was in the drama race, then moved to comedy.

	In 2015, the Academy shifted the rules: All half hours would be classified as comedies and all hourlong shows would have to submit as dramas. But shows could petition to switch fields, and so many did that the confusion led the org to raise the white flag and get rid of those classifications by 2022. Now, a show can enter whatever it feels like. That’s why you have so many comedic drama entrants and dramatic comedy contenders.

	Maybe we should go back to how things were handled in 1957: For one year there was no “comedy” or “drama race” — just “best series, half-hour or less” and “best series, one hour or more.” But even that didn’t work: In the hourlong field, comedy “Caesar’s Hour” was pitted against “Ed Sullivan” and the arts show “Omnibus,” while in half hour, the comedy “Phil Silvers Show” was up against thriller “Alfred Hitchcock Presents” and the news show “Person to Person.” 
	

	What’s a comedy?

schema.headline: ‘Widow’s Bay’ and Other Contenders Continue to Complicate Emmy’s Comedy Conundrum

title: ‘Slow Horses’ Actor Jack Lowden Unpacks River Cartwright and Why Pride Gets in His Way
description: It’s fair to say that when audiences see River Cartwright at the beginning of Apple TV’s “Slow Horses” Season 5, he is not in a good place. The prev
body:
It’s fair to say that when audiences see River Cartwright at the beginning of Apple TV’s “Slow Horses” Season 5, he is not in a good place. The previous season revealed that River’s father, Frank Harkness (Hugo Weaving), is both a sociopath and the leader of a network of trained assassins. It was also revealed that Frank had fathered numerous sons and raised them to carry out his hits.

	“I think for anybody, that would be quite traumatic,” says Jack Lowden of his character River’s damage, which carries into Season 5; his base of operations, MI5’s Slough House headed by Gary Oldman’s Jackson Lamb, has become a bit too much for him.
	

	“When I was filming that season and Season 6, my grandfather is at the forefront of my mind. I feel like that begins to overtake his ambition because he wants to make his grandfather proud,” says Lowden. “He’s not in the best of head space, and he’s thinner physically. I think nerves-wise, he’s thinner. I don’t think he’s particularly in a happy place or particularly well, so to speak.”

	Lowden details peeling back the layers of River and why the character ends up in a much more hopeful place as the show heads into its sixth season.



	

	


	
		Let’s get right to it. In Episode 5, “Circus,” River is lying to Jackson about the death of politician Dennis Gimball (Christopher Villiers). Take us into his mind. Why does he lie?	

	What I’ve always found interesting about River is his pride, because I find pride in people incredibly petty, and it pushes people to do stupid things for the sake of how they look or how they come across. He’s trying not to look bad. This season, he’s not in a great head space. I love the fact that, no matter that his personal life is falling apart, at the end of the day, at work, he still doesn’t want to look stupid.
	
	
		You’ve said River’s grandfather, played so brilliantly by Jonathan Pryce, impacts a big part of his actions. What were those garden scenes like when they have a heart-to-heart?	

	Jonathan and I talk about that quite a lot — losing someone is horrific, and the grief is terrible. But you are watching someone in front of you disappear slowly, with the terrible disease of Alzheimer’s or dementia. I’ve not experienced it yet, but I can imagine it’s horrific. On top of that, his grandfather is his hero. He’s also trying to emulate his grandfather and follow in his footsteps, and to watch him evaporate in front of him is terrible. But in true “Slow Horses” fashion, David will still give him a little seed of something that will sort of open up the entire thing for him. I took that as a real moment of hope. I think, in the moment, River is very much focused on the problem at hand. But when you get someone who hasthat condition, and there are these little kernels of hope that they are still who they were — it’s just so moving. I think I actually found that a hopeful scene. But again, playing with somebody like Jonathan Pryce, I would be lying if I said I completely stayed in River’s head space.
	
		How do you prepare for something that’s so heavy for this character? 	

	I tend to stay away from those moments as much as possible. I try to come at them from as jolly and playful a place as I can, because I think that’s true to what happens in life. When you’re faced with grief, sadness or tragedy, you’re trying really hard not to give in to the terribleness of the situation. So I tried todo that with these scenes. I don’t spend the night before pushing myself into a certain state. The challenge of just instantly trying to put yourself in that situation and using your imagination — at the end of the day, that’s what I feel makes it fun.



	

	


	
		By the end of the season, River thinks that he’s finally got his ticket out of Slough House. Instead, Lamb makes sure River stays at Slough House. Where would you say River is at the end of the season? 	

	As far as he’s concerned, he’s pulled off a lot of impressive feats. In particular, the saving of James Callis’ character was meant to give River that moment of feeling like he’s earned his place, gotten his stripes back, and just needs to go to Lamb. He has the chance for a promotion and lays it at the door of whatis probably the worst boss in history. River and Lamb are intrinsically linked, but they’re often kept apart, which makes their interactions more special when they do happen. There’s more respect for Lamb now, but I do think we leave River in a more hopeful place than where he was at the beginning of the season. I’m glad about that because, during this season in particular, he’s not exactly a happy bunny.
	
	
		What has it been like peeling back the layers of this character over the seasons?	

	 It’s an interesting question, because this is the only experience I’ve had doing anything recurring for this long. I find it incredibly hard, whenever I do watch the show, to differentiate myself from River because I’m also watching a guy who was 29, I think, when I began. I’m now 36, and the world has been through a lot in that time. Everybody has. I find it quite interesting to just watch someone growing up — not just River, but myself. I think what I’ve enjoyed is seeing myself grow up as an actor as well. It’s why I still act. It’s not necessarily because I want to play all the great characters — though, of course, there are people I want to work with and still haven’t worked with. But I go to work every day because I want to get better at what I do. I feel incredibly lucky as an actor that this is a profession you can learn to master, even though you probably never will. I can see my progression. I remember how I was feeling on a certain day. I remember the difference in how it felt in Season 1 compared to Season 5. I just see a boy who’s sort of eventually becoming a man. Hopefully.
	
		Who are some of those actors you’d like to work with? Let’s manifest. 	

	Matthew Macfadyen; he’s a benchmark for me. I find his range remarkable. I think he’s phenomenal, and I would desperately love to work with him. Last year, I was very fortunate to work with Martin Freeman. He is another actor that I think has incredible range and has a severely sharp technical ability that I got to see up close night after night.

schema.headline: ‘Slow Horses’ Actor Jack Lowden Unpacks River Cartwright and Why Pride Gets in His Way

title: Telemundo Executive José Suárez Dies in Helicopter Crash at 55
description: José Alberto Suárez, president and general manager of Telemundo‘s TV stations in Orlando, Tampa and Fort Myers-Naples, Florida, died Wednesday in a
body:
José Alberto Suárez, president and general manager of Telemundo‘s TV stations in Orlando, Tampa and Fort Myers-Naples, Florida, died Wednesday in a helicopter crash, according to the NBCUniversal-owned broadcaster. He was 55.

	Suárez was one of four Americans who died in a helicopter crash in Samburu County in northeastern Kenya, according to NBC’s Miami station. All seven people aboard the aircraft, including the pilot, were killed, NBC News’ “Today” reported.
	

	In a memo to employees, NBCUniversal News Group chairman Cesar Conde, NBCU Local chairman Valari Staab and Telemundo station group president Jose Cancela said: “We are heartbroken to share the tragic news that José Suárez, the president and general manager of the Telemundo-owned stations in Orlando, Tampa and Fort Myers, was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya. José was a deeply respected leader and beloved friend and colleague across NBCU Local and NBCU News Group.”


	The memo continued, “José was an exceptional colleague and mentor to many. He cared deeply about his teams, the communities they served and the essential role our stations play in people’s lives. He brought energy, humor, warmth and a strong sense of purpose to his work, and his impact was felt far beyond the stations he led. The suddenness and circumstances of José’s passing make this loss especially difficult to comprehend. Our hearts are with his loved ones, and with all of José’s colleagues and friends across NBCUniversal who are grieving this terrible loss. We will share more about how we will honor José’s life and legacy in the days ahead.”
	

	Suárez worked for NBCU in multiple roles over the course of 20 years, including leading stations in San Antonio, Sacramento, Fresno, Salt Lake City and Las Vegas. Most recently, he was GM of Telemundo 31 (Orlando), Telemundo 49 (Tampa) and Telemundo Ft. Myers-Naples. 

	Before becoming a station leader, Suárez was director of creative services and programming for NBC’s WTVJ in Miami. Earlier, he had held digital media roles with the NBC 6 in Miami and Telemundo 51. Before joining NBCU, Suárez held news and on-air roles for media outlets in Florida, Ohio and Texas. He had been a member of the National Association of Hispanic Journalists since 1998, according to his LinkedIn profile.

	Suárez received multiple honors during his career, including the 2019 Lone Star Emmy for overall excellence while he was president and GM of Telemundo 60 San Antonio; a Suncoast Chapter Emmy award for outstanding station promotion image with NBC 6; three Cleveland-chapter Emmys for outstanding daily newscast; and several AP awards for his work at Fox Toledo/WUPW.

schema.headline: Telemundo Executive José Suárez Dies in Helicopter Crash at 55

Nolan Wells' Friends

                              August 19, 2026
                            1:12 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Nolan Wells would have turned 19 today ... and three of the friends who were with him before his death joined a virtual vigil honoring his life.
      
    
            Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo and Morgan Seymour participated in the National Action Network's noon prayer vigil for Nolan ... appearing on Zoom with their cameras on and microphones muted.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Attorney Edward Andrew Paltzik, who represents the three friends, tells TMZ ... they wanted to honor Nolan on his birthday ... and he shared a statement from the young men.
      

            It reads ... "On this special day, August 19, just like every day, we honor and remember our dear friend, Nolan Wells. He was the brightest of lights who touched many lives, including ours. His memory will shine on in our hearts. Always."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Rev. Al Sharpton even acknowledged the trio's presence during the livestream. He had promoted the vigil beforehand ... asking people nationwide to pray for Nolan's loved ones, honor his life, and stand with his family as they continue seeking "truth, transparency and justice."
      
    
            As we previously reported ... Nolan disappeared from Mississippi's Horn Island during a July 4 outing with friends. His body was discovered along the island's shoreline two days later, near where he was last seen alive.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Warren, Jax and Morgan have since publicly maintained they had nothing to do with Nolan's death ... and have pushed back against accusations and threats they've faced in the weeks since.
      
    
            Nolan's death remains under investigation ... but Wednesday, the focus was on the birthday he never got to celebrate.
